claim: The Yale (or Harvard) study where the 3% who wrote down their goals out-earned the other 97%
why: The study does not exist. Yale has no record of it. Fast Company chased it to its source in 1996 and found nothing. It is repeated constantly in coaching.
sayInstead: Gail Matthews' 2015 Dominican University study is real, was actually run, and found written goals plus accountability improved achievement. Use that one and cite it.

claim: It takes 21 days to form a habit
why: From Maxwell Maltz's Psycho-Cybernetics (1960), an observation about how long amputees took to stop feeling a phantom limb. Never a habit study. Lally et al. 2010 found a median of 66 days with enormous variation.
sayInstead: Habits take longer than people expect, and how long varies enormously by person and behaviour.

why: Mehrabian's research is real but was about people judging feelings when the words and the tone contradicted each other. It was never a claim about communication in general. Mehrabian himself has said so repeatedly.
sayInstead: When your words and your delivery disagree, people believe the delivery.

claim: The human attention span is now 8 seconds, shorter than a goldfish
why: Traced to a Microsoft report that cited a source which did not contain the claim. No researcher has ever measured a goldfish's attention span.
sayInstead: People decide fast whether something is for them. Earn the first line.

claim: It takes 7 touches to make a sale
why: No source has ever been produced. The number is also given as 5, 8, 12 and 13 depending on who is selling what.
sayInstead: Familiarity lowers resistance — and that one is real. Zajonc 1968, already in your Evidence shelf.

claim: The average person sees 5,000 (or 10,000) ads a day
why: Traced to a single unsourced 2007 quote in a newspaper article. Repeated ever since, never measured.
sayInstead: People see a great deal of marketing and most of it does not register.

pattern: 10% of what they read|learning pyramid|cone of learning|retain 90%
claim: People remember 10% of what they read, 20% of what they hear, 90% of what they do
why: The 'learning pyramid' or 'cone of learning'. The numbers were invented; they conveniently descend in multiples of ten. Repeatedly traced and repeatedly found to have no study behind them.
sayInstead: Doing something is a better way to learn it than reading about it.

claim: 90% of businesses fail in the first year
why: Real survival data exists and does not say this. Roughly 20% of US businesses close in year one and about half within five years. The 90% figure is a scare number.
sayInstead: Cite the actual survival figures, or drop the statistic and describe what you see instead.

claim: It costs 5x more to acquire a customer than to keep one
why: Cited everywhere with no primary source. The multiple is variously given as 4x, 5x, 6x, 7x and 25x. It also varies enormously by industry, so a single number cannot be true.
sayInstead: Keeping a client is usually cheaper than finding a new one, and by how much depends on your business.

why: A misreading of an IRS statistic about the number of income categories on high-earner tax returns. Not a strategy anyone measured.
sayInstead: Nothing. Say what you have actually seen work.

why: Attributed to a 'Marketing Donut' page that cited no study. Reproduced in thousands of sales decks since.
sayInstead: Most people do not buy the first time you ask. Follow up more than feels comfortable.

pattern: left brain|right brain|creative side of the brain
why: Not how brains work. There are no left-dominant or right-dominant personality types; imaging studies find no such split.
sayInstead: People approach problems differently, and it is not because of which half of their brain they use.
